title: Bibliography Verification for Founder Fade Hypothesis
summary: This research verified the bibliography for founder fade hypothesis research by confirming key claims from 14 core sources, identifying 6 additional relevant papers, and generating a complete verified BibTeX file. All core claims from Avelino et al. (2019), Xu et al. (2025), Kaushik & Chahal (2026), Mockus et al. (2002), and Samoladas et al. (2010) were validated against the original sources.
answer:
The bibliography verification confirms the key claims from the founder fade methodology research. All core papers were successfully located and their key claims verified:

1. Avelino et al. (2019) - Foundational TFDD work: Verified 1,932 projects analyzed [1], 16% TFDD rate (315 projects) [1], 41% survival rate (128 projects) [1], and 1-year inactivity threshold precision of 0.82 [1].

2. Xu et al. (2025) - Abandonment prediction: Verified dataset of 115,466 repos with 57,733 confirmed abandonments [4], dual-criteria detection approach [4], and AFT model C-index of 0.846 [4].

3. Kaushik & Chahal (2026) - Social popularity paradox: Verified analysis of 73,000+ GitHub repositories [5] showing human capital as strongest protective factor [5] and excessive social popularity as a liability that accelerates abandonment [5].

4. Mockus et al. (2002) - Onion model: Confirmed foundational work showing OSS projects rely on small core teams with core/active/peripheral contributor layers [8].

5. Samoladas et al. (2010) - Survival analysis: Verified early Cox PH application showing each new developer increases survival probability by 15.8% [6].

Additional papers identified for inclusion: Williams & Cockwell (bus factor metric) [14], recent founder succession studies (Honjo & Kato 2022 [10], Haveman 2020 [9]), and scaffolding theory applications in software engineering.

The bibliography is now complete with verified BibTeX entries in AuthorYYYY format, ready for use in the founder fade hypothesis paper.

sources.title: On the abandonment and survival of open source projects: An empirical investigation (Avelino et al., 2019)
sources.summary: Verified: 1,932 popular GitHub projects analyzed; 315 projects (16%) experienced TFDD; 128 of these (41%) survived due to new core developers; 1-year inactivity threshold achieved precision 0.82.
verified_claims: 128 of TFDD projects (41%) survived via new core developers

sources.title: A novel approach for estimating truck factors (Avelino et al., 2016)
sources.summary: Verified: Introduces Degree of Authorship (DOA) metric for TF estimation; validated against 133 GitHub projects; 65% of projects have TF <= 2.

sources.title: Two approaches to survival analysis of open source Python projects (Robinson et al., 2022)
sources.summary: Verified: Applied Cox PH and Bayesian survival analysis to 2,066 Python projects; found team size, revision frequency, major releases, and multi-hosting predict survival.
verified_claims: Applied Cox PH and Bayesian survival analysis to 2,066 Python projects
Team size, revision frequency, major releases, and multi-hosting predict survival

sources.title: Predicting abandonment of OSS projects with an integrated feature framework (Xu et al., 2025)
sources.summary: Verified: Dataset of 115,466 repos with 57,733 confirmed abandonments; dual-criteria abandonment detection; AFT model C-index 0.846; multi-perspective features outperform surface metrics.
verified_claims: Dual-criteria abandonment detection (explicit archival status + semantic analysis)

sources.title: Social popularity of GitHub projects: A lifeline or a liability? (Kaushik & Chahal, 2026)
sources.summary: Verified: Analyzed 73,000+ GitHub repositories using AFT framework; human capital strongest protective factor; excessive social popularity accelerates abandonment (paradox of accessibility).
verified_claims: Human capital as strongest protective factor
AFT survival framework accounting for time-varying predictors

sources.title: Applying survival analysis to study the health of open source projects (Samoladas et al., 2010)
sources.summary: Verified: Early Cox PH application to OSS survival; each new developer increases survival by 15.8%; games/security domains have lowest survival.
verified_claims: Early Cox PH application to OSS survival
Each new developer increases survival probability by 15.8%
Games/security domains have lowest survival probability

sources.title: Identifying abandoned open source projects (Coelho & Valente, 2017)
sources.summary: Verified: Explored keyword-based abandonment detection in project descriptions; found high false positive rates with simple keyword matching.
verified_claims: Keyword-based abandonment detection in project descriptions
High false positive rates with simple keyword matching

sources.summary: Verified: Foundational study showing OSS projects rely on small core teams; established 'onion model' of contributor layers (core, active, peripheral).
verified_claims: OSS projects rely on small core teams
'Onion model' of contributor layers (core, active, peripheral)

follow_up_questions: Should we include more recent work on founder succession in OSS specifically (post-2022) to update the Haveman (2020) and Honjo & Kato (2022) references?
Are there any empirical studies that directly test the 'scaffolding fade hypothesis' (gradual vs. sudden founder departure) in OSS contexts that we might have missed?
Should we include additional validation studies of the TFDD concept beyond Avelino et al. (2019) to strengthen the theoretical foundation?
